claims.text: Traditional kaiseki cooking here relies on standard Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, miso, dashi); no wheat-free soy sauce or gluten-free protocol is documented, so wheat exposure should be assumed unless arranged.
The standard omakase includes Yamato beef, Yamato chicken and fish/dashi, so dishes are not vegan or vegetarian by default and would need to be specially prepared on request.
Reservation-only fixed omakase with a small kitchen; the chef's shōjin background suggests plant-based or dietary courses can sometimes be arranged, but only if requested in advance when booking.
Chef trained as the opening head chef of a two-Michelin-star shōjin (vegetarian) restaurant, so the kitchen genuinely understands plant-based Japanese cooking when given notice.
Hand-made wheat udon is the central product and is prepared on-site, so flour and gluten are pervasive throughout the kitchen; this is not a safe environment for celiacs.
Dishes are built around fish/meat-based broths and toppings (tori tempura, chicken-and-egg, offal miso, beef stew), so shared broth and cooking surfaces make vegan cross-contact likely.
The shop's listing invites guests to contact them directly with any questions, but no specific allergy-handling procedures are documented.

name: うどん 一期一会 (Udon Ichigo-Ichie)

claims.text: A wheat-udon specialist: the noodles are wheat and are boiled in shared water; any tempura toppings are wheat-battered. Cross-contamination with gluten is inherent — not a celiac-safe kitchen.
Udon tsuyu is made with Japanese soy sauce, which typically contains wheat; the dashi/tare should be assumed to contain gluten unless the shop confirms otherwise.

The dashi is a sweet katsuo/kombu-style broth (assume bonito) and the signature niku-udon uses beef, so most bowls carry animal ingredients. A bonito-free bowl would need to be requested and confirmed.
A tiny owner-run counter where the noodles are made in front of you, so you can ask about the dashi and ingredients directly before ordering.
Products are deep-fried satsuma-age/kamaboko; surimi fish cakes typically contain wheat starch or flour as a binder, and frying is done in shared oil. No gluten-free handling is documented.
Shop recommends eating the fried cakes with grated daikon and soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
All items are fish-based surimi products; there are no vegan items and everything shares fish-paste preparation and frying.

name: ヴィーガンカフェ 楽夢菜 (Vegan Cafe Ramuna (Rakumuna))

claims.text: Bread, cakes and tarts are baked in-house from whole-grain wheat flour and the savory menu includes soy-meat items and a shoyu (wheat) ramen, so wheat is present across the kitchen with no dedicated GF setup.
Menu includes a shoyu ramen; standard soy sauce contains wheat. Seasonings are traditionally-made organic but not stated to be wheat-free.
Entirely plant-based kitchen with no animal products used (no meat, fish, dairy, egg, gelatin or honey), so cross-contact with animal ingredients is not a concern.
Will accommodate gokun-nuki (preparation without the five pungent alliums) on request.
100% vegan, whole-foods kitchen using organic, additive-free ingredients and no refined sugar, so vegan diners can order anything on the menu with confidence.
English menu available to help international visitors order.

name: Vegan Ramen by Playpen Friends（ヴィーガンラーメン専門店） (Vegan Ramen by Playpen Friends)

claims.text: Ramen noodles are wheat-based and the menu is wheat- and broth-heavy; no dedicated gluten-free handling is documented, so the kitchen should be treated as not celiac-safe.
Soy-sauce and miso ramen styles are offered; standard Japanese soy sauce and miso contain wheat and no wheat-free version is documented.
The same kitchen cooks genuine pork-bone and chicken-paitan ramen alongside the vegan bowls, so shared-equipment cross-contact is possible; strict vegans should confirm handling.
Around six clearly labeled vegan ramen options make it easy for plant-based diners to order without ambiguity.
Vegan miso bowl is built on a domestic miso base with vegetables stir-fried in plant oil and plant-based toppings (fried tofu, soy meat, seaweed, vegetables).

name: vegan soba 楽夢咲 (Vegan Soba Ramusa)

claims.text: Soba is offered as a 100% buckwheat (十割) or 80/20 buckwheat-wheat (二八) blend, and the set includes wheat-battered vegetable tempura, so wheat is present and cross-contamination is likely.
The entire shop is plant-based, so vegan diners can order the full menu without modification.

name: 若草カレー本舗 (Wakakusa Curry Honpo)

claims.text: The kitchen makes curry bread and curry ramen and uses wheat-based curry roux, so wheat is handled heavily; no dedicated gluten-free preparation or equipment is documented.
Vegetarian curries are cooked in a kitchen that also prepares chicken, beef, and lamb curries; shared equipment and stock are not addressed in available materials.
Offers a purpose-made vegetarian Veg Wakakusa Curry of sesame and vegetables, including an onion- and garlic-free version for Buddhist-style diets.
Official site advertises vegetarian/vegan and gluten-free, pork-free menu options.
